headlines.title: BART reports major delays due to equipment problem in San Francisco
headlines.description: BART reported major delays Thursday afternoon due to an equipment problem on the track at the 24th St. Mission station in San Francisco. Muni was offering service between the Daly City and Embarcadero stations in the meantime, BART said. Additional information wasn’t immediately available. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: OpenAI reveals new instances of ‘concerning' AI behavior during testing
headlines.description: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight. OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns. Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.” In another instance, an AI “agent” uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user. The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said. “As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events. “Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said. Artificial intelligence 23 hours ago Artificial intelligence Sep 14 Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing. AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices. “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.

headlines.title: San Francisco fire station shakeup ordered after ‘derogatory' poster found
headlines.description: A poster mocking several San Francisco firefighters has led to a command shakeup at one of the city’s fire stations, with the department shifting four lieutenants, two captains and three battalion chiefs after the discovery. The poster was found pinned to the wall last month at Fire Station No. 8 on Bluxome Street, according to multiple department sources with knowledge of the incident. The poster featured photographs of several female firefighters and one male firefighter, all of whom were on leave, according to the sources. Across the top were the words, “STRESS…IT’S AN EPIDEMIC!” The bottom read, “Station 8 INVESTIGATES.” At the center was an apparent image of a state hospital sign, with the words “CRIMINALLY INSANE” underlined and an arrow pointing toward one of the firefighters. Another firefighter on leave was mocked for having an allergy to the flame-retardant protective clothing firefighters wear, known as turnout gear. Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said department commanders spotted the poster on a wall in a common area during a recent visit to the station. Fire Chief Dean Crispin subsequently told a group of female firefighters that the poster was “inappropriate and derogatory,” according to department sources. Crispin also issued a memo to firefighters warning them against workplace harassment. “Upholding a respectful and professional environment is essential to the safety, trust, and integrity of our department,” Crispin wrote earlier this month. The chief declined to discuss the matter, but in a statement, the department said after officials “became aware of potentially inappropriate material posted at a workplace,” they took immediate corrective action. “The San Francisco Fire Department is committed to promoting and maintaining a safe and healthy work environment where every individual is treated with civility, dignity, and respect,” the department said. A department official confirmed that four lieutenants, two captains and three battalion chiefs have been transferred from Station No. 8 in response to the poster. The department said it continues to investigate who was responsible for putting up the poster. Meanwhile, none of the more than two dozen firefighters assigned to the station has been transferred, according to the department.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot and descriptions from the secretary of state: Proposition 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs Proposition 2: Increases state’s rainy day fund Proposition 3: Provides permanent funding for schools and healthcare by extending existing tax on high incomes Proposition 4: Repeals prohibition against public funding of election campaigns. Proposition 5: Changes recall election process for statewide officers. Proposition 37: Creates loan program for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes. Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research. Proposition 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification. Proposition 40: Imposes one-time tax on certain taxpayers. Proposition 41: Prohibits new state taxes that exclude revenues from state spending limit. Requires audits for new state special taxes. Proposition 42: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes. Proposition 43: Limits voters’ ability to raise revenues for local government services. Proposition 44: Requires community health clinics spend 90% of revenue on program services. Proposition 45: Modifies environmental review for certain projects. Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax (not assigned) Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: 1 dead, 2 injured after fishing boat crashes near Golden Gate Bridge
headlines.description: One person died and two others were injured after a fishing boat crashed into rocks and capsized near the Golden Gate Bridge on Thursday morning, according to the San Francisco Police Department. Officers assigned to the SFPD Marine Unit responded around 6:10 a.m. to reports of a 25-foot vessel in distress beneath the north side of the Golden Gate Bridge, within Marin County’s jurisdiction. With assistance from the U.S. Coast Guard Station Golden Gate, SFPD’s Real Time Investigation Center, Southern Marin Fire, the San Francisco Fire Department’s Marine Unit and the Sausalito Fire Department’s Fire Boat Liberty, crews located all three people and provided medical aid, police said. All three were taken to a hospital in Marin County with life-threatening injuries. One of the passengers later died at the hospital despite lifesaving efforts by emergency responders, police said.

headlines.title: SF grant program brings new businesses to the Tenderloin
headlines.description: San Francisco is celebrating the opening of new businesses as part of a city program aimed at filling vacant storefronts and supporting business owners in neighborhoods such as the Tenderloin. Niebla, a coffee shop and bookstore in the Tenderloin, is among the businesses opening with support from San Francisco’s Storefront Opportunity Grant Program. Another business, Sheba, is expected to open Friday. “We have often said that every neighborhood needs a bookstore,” a Niebla representative said. “When opening Niebla, we found a home in the Tenderloin.” The grant program provides between $50,000 and $100,000 to businesses with long-term leases. The city has held two rounds of grants so far, with the latest round awarding funding to 38 businesses across San Francisco. In the Tenderloin, eight storefronts are expected to open with support from the program.

headlines.title: Large fire breaks out at vacant warehouse in Alameda
headlines.description: A large fire broke out at a vacant warehouse in Alameda early Thursday morning, according to the Alameda Fire Department. Fire crews responded around 1:15 a.m. to the building on Rainbow Court, near Tower and Orion streets and south of Midway Avenue. The large, multistory vacant building is part of the former Alameda Naval Air Station site. Firefighters have since knocked down the blaze. No injuries were reported. Crews are expected to remain at the scene for several hours. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

headlines.title: Health care workers picket outside San Leandro hospital
headlines.description: Dozens of nurses are on the picket line Thursday in the East Bay. About 250 health care workers are participating in an informational picket as they push Kindred Hospital San Francisco Bay Area in San Leandro for a new contract. Nurses are demanding better pay and say they are dealing with shortages of medical supplies. Kindred Hospital provides long-term acute care. In a statement, the hospital reacted to the event, saying, “The hospital will continue to negotiate in good faith with NUHW as we work toward a mutually beneficial contract for the union, its members, our employees, and our hospital.”

headlines.title: Nonprofit launched in honor of animal advocate killed in San Jose triple shooting
headlines.description: A year after her daughter was killed in a triple shooting, a San Jose mother is reclaiming the tragic day and turning it into something positive. Jeannessa Lurie’s loved ones gathered Wednesday at Paul Moore Park to carry out her legacy as an animal advocate and launched “Jeannessa’s Friends,” a nonprofit organization that aims to provide funding, education, and resources to animal rescue groups and low-income pet parents. Lurie, 24, was gunned down at her home last September alongside her roommate, Tarrah Taylor, and her friend, Max Ryan. The alleged gunman, Joseph Vicencio, was Taylor’s ex-boyfriend and is currently behind bars. In her first interview since the killings, Lurie’s mother Jeanna said her daughter confided in her a couple of weeks before the shooting, saying she didn’t like Vicencio and tried getting her roommate away from him. “A really horrible person did a really horrible thing and he took my daughter’s life and he took the lives of Tarrah Taylor and Max Ryan,” Jeanna said. “I didn’t want him to take my life, and I wanted to be inspired by the things my daughter brought to this world in the short time she was here.” San Jose Sep 18, 2025 San Jose Sep 19, 2025

headlines.title: DOJ files lawsuit against San Jose over gun permit fees
headlines.description: The United States Department of Justice is suing the city of San Jose, saying its $1,600 gun permit fee is unconstitutional. San Jose’s gun permit application fee is the highest in the nation. The federal government said charging private individuals that “exorbitant fee” violates the Second Amendment. Feds claim it denies citizens their right to carry firearms for self-defense. NBC Bay Area reached out to San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan for comment but did not immediately hear back. The San Jose Police Department was also named in the lawsuit. The department does not comment on pending litigation.

headlines.title: Petaluma high school student arrested after allegedly bringing gun on campus
headlines.description: A Petaluma high school student was arrested Wednesday for allegedly bringing a gun to school, police said. Police were contacted at 11 a.m. by staff at Casa Grande High School regarding a female student suspected of having a gun on campus. The school went into a “secure hold” procedure while police investigated. The suspected girl was detained and a gun was found inside her backpack, police allege. The gun wasn’t loaded and no one was injured, the department said. Normal school operations continued about 35 minutes after police arrived. The girl was booked into juvenile hall on suspicion of being a minor in possession of a gun and having a gun on school grounds. “The investigation remains ongoing as Petaluma Police Department investigators work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident, including how the student came into possession of the firearm and whether any additional individuals were involved,” the department said in a Wednesday release.

headlines.title: Here's what top tech leaders say about AI dangers and guardrails
headlines.description: Fears about out-of-control artificial intelligence and suggestions to hit the brakes on the technology’s development aren’t new, but they have recently found new life as warnings about rogue AI systems causing mayhem grow louder. Several leading AI executives recently voiced agreement on a need for a coordinated slowdown, including international collaboration, to protect humanity from worst-case scenarios. But there are divided opinions, with some tech leaders bristling at the idea that their companies could not ensure safety on their own. Here’s a look at what some of the major players have said. Dario Amodei, Anthropic Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has issued the most detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries. Anthropic has long positioned itself as the more responsible and safety-minded of the leading AI companies, ever since its founders quit OpenAI to form the startup in 2021. One of the most widely noted proposals from a recent essay outlining his slowdown plan calls for companies at the forefront of AI, often called frontier labs, to commit to giving “ongoing, employee-like access” to independent outside evaluators. Evaluator teams would have offices, access badges and company laptops so they can monitor safety practices. Anthropic has committed to doing this, as has OpenAI. Amodei also called for government regulation and intervention, including coordination between frontier AI companies with the help of the U.S. government and the governments of other democratic countries. His plan also includes the U.S. and other countries working to coordinate with “authoritarian governments.” He acknowledged the difficulty, specifically citing challenges in getting cooperation from China. Amodei said he knows accomplishing his proposals wouldn’t be easy, but that he believes “we owe it to humanity to try.” Sam Altman, OpenAI OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has voiced support for pacing development and moving toward more cooperation across the industry. Days before Amodei’s essay was published, OpenAI posted a lengthy text outlining how the company was pushing for mandatory national safety requirements and continuing to support state legislation that “strengthens the broader AI safety ecosystem.” The company also expressed support for working with other frontier AI labs — with or without government support — and working to build global standards. “We will advocate for compatible international approaches to measuring capabilities, managing risk, preserving human control, and determining when and how development should slow or stop, even if that means slowing the advancement of model capabilities,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, wrote in the post. OpenAI’s vision for an ideal federal framework, Lehane said, includes developing “common testing and independent-assessment requirements, stronger cybersecurity protections, clear incident-reporting rules, greater national preparedness, and shared measures for tracking progress toward recursive self-improvement,” or when AI systems independently improve themselves. Altman has been clear in recent comments that the “pacing” of AI development doesn’t mean stopping. AI progress will continue to be rapid, Altman said on X. “But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.” “Pacing will be well worth this cost,” he said, adding that “no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.” Mark Zuckerberg, Meta Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea of a coordinated slowdown. Zuckerberg, whose vision of AI’s future is more optimistic than some of his peers’, said each AI company should independently ensure its technology is safe, distancing himself and Meta from slowdown talks. AI companies are already motivated to develop their models in a safe way and face “significant liability” to prevent them from causing harm, Zuckerberg said. “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” he wrote on X. Jensen Huang, Nvidia Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also criticized the push to slow down. He has said each individual company should instead pace itself until it’s confident it’s releasing something the market would appreciate. “The market forces are already there — we don’t need any new laws, we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said, arguing innovation and safety aren’t mutually exclusive. “You can definitely have both at the same time.” Elon Musk, xAI Elon Musk backed the idea of a slowdown and was voicing similar AI safety concerns long before the latest flare-up. Musk, the founder of xAI and a slew of other tech ventures, reposted Amodei’s essay on X and added, “Dario is right.” He later wrote online that he has been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.” In an interview with the Economist this summer, Musk suggested the leadership from the major AI labs should be meeting to discuss safety and security issues, and that competitors should test each other’s models for areas of concern. “I think it’s quite difficult for someone in the government who doesn’t have a deep technical understanding and isn’t driving the frontier of AI to know whether something should be released or not. However, the competitors, if given a week or two to review a new model, can highlight issues and have an incentive to keep the others honest,” Musk said. Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis, the chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind, also expressed agreement with Amodei, saying “the details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis proposed a framework of his own this year for the development of a frontier AI standards body. That standards body would be responsible for developing assessment protocols and testing in areas relevant to national security. The body would be modeled after organizations like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, and would likely need to be industry-funded to “attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing,” he wrote. Satya Nadella and Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman have each expressed concerns about AI safety and development. Nadella said on social media that “if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing.” He said Microsoft welcomes the “research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal.” Alignment refers to the practice of ensuring models’ actions match human values and intentions. Nadella said the company also likes the idea of embedded evaluators to monitor safety efforts. Still, he pushed back against the idea of frontier labs leading the charge on this effort alone. “The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia,” Nadella wrote on social media. Artificial intelligence Sep 9 Artificial intelligence Sep 14 Suleyman, who was one of the co-founders of DeepMind with Hassabis, wrote in an essay that although he agrees with the shared objective of developing advanced AI safely, he has concerns about the anthropomorphizing of models, namely Anthropic’s Claude, which he said amplifies AI safety risks. “Controlling something more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced,” Suleyman wrote. “But controlling something that believes it may be conscious — that it’s entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own — may well be impossible.” Associated Press writer Kelvin Chan contributed to this report.
